maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Tuesday, February 26, consideration erf the motion of the Minister of Finance that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself again into committee of supply, and on the proposed amendment of Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver).
Mr. JOHN T. HACKETT (Stanstead): At adjournment last evening I had told the house that unemployment exists only in the large cities of the dominion. I had suggested that there are in these cities half a million workers who are without work, and I was about to inquire how this surplus population had found its way into the cities. The answer is probably twofold. The first is to be found in our immigration policy. For many years we have welcomed to our shores people of varied vocations and of varied training. It is true that most of those who came here immediately before the depression were classified as farmers or farm labourers, but a careful scrutiny of those who arrived between 1925 and 1930 will show very clearly that a substantial percentage of them either remained in the cities or found their way there shortly after their arrival, attracted by the high wages and other incidentals of city existence. For the ten years which preceded 1930 about 150,000 people a year were received into the dominion, or about a million and a half. The second reason for the surplus population in the cities is to be found in the trend of population from rural sections to the cities. Fifty years ago only eighteen per cent of the population of Canada

resided in urban centres; in 1931 about fifty-four per cent of the total population of Canada resided in the cities.
If in these centres there are half a million workers for whom there is no work, and we consider that these half million workers and their dependents constitute at least a tithe of our population, it would seem to me to be a very prudent thing to inquire whether there is any reason to anticipate that there will be employment for these workless people in a future which is not too remote. We have heard economic nationalism, national self-sufficiency, criticized in this house; and we have heard scathing references made to those who practise it. But whether we like it or not, it is a fact, and it is one which is well established in all countries of the world. It is one which we as well as others are practising. It is a doctrine which has its foundation in a very human and very natural sentiment. When there is not bread enough for the whole company we feed our own family first. I suggest therefore that unless we can see some hope of employing in gainful work those who are out of work in our cities, and of doing so in the immediate future, it behooves us to consider very carefully whether they may not have to 'be removed to other places where they can earn at least their own food and where they will cease to be dependent on the other nine-tenths of the population of the country.
We have heard a great deal of the woes of the unemployed. I do not think that the Conservative party or any member in this house is unaware of the embarrassment of the man who is without employment and without the means of sustaining his family. But after all there is another element in the community about whom we have not heard so much. We have heard a great deal about the man without a job, but it is about time something was said of the man with a job who is bearing the burden of the troubles that are weighing so heavily upon the country to-day. We find that the burden of maintaining the unemployed has become very heavy and it is making itself felt in the large centres to such an extent that our eities are on the verge of bankruptcy and are resorting to all manner of expedients to support those who are out of work. It seems to me that we should recognize the fact that a country cannot exist or persist if its cities cease to perform their allotted functions. The cities are the great pulsating organs of the national life and by them the blood of trade commerce and policy is put into circulation. If the cities become bankrupt and are unable to

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Hackett
perform this function necessary to national existence, the nation as a whole is bound to suffer if not to perish.
I have noticed that the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) has not given any credit to the government for enacting policies which I think admittedly have not only made our situation better but in any event have prevented it from becoming as difficult as the situation is in other countries. I believe the policy which raised tariffs and gave employment to our own people was a beneficent one and one which was helpful to the Canadian people as a whole. I believe the policy which closed our doors to immigration and negotiated trade treaties, was wise and useful, but I was amazed that the hon. members entirely overlooked the policy of land settlement which has been practised by the government and which has achieved very substantial success. It has not been hearalded abroad as widely as have some of the other activities of the government. I have before me a statement of the work accomplished by the Department of Labour showing a situation which I think should arrest the attention of the house. I find that from October 1, 1930, to December 31, 1934, no less than 132,444 people have been taken from the cities and established on the soil or in work on the soil. Families settled on farms at no expense at all to the government number 15,589 and comprise 77,945 persons. Single men placed in farm work number 33,842, making a total of 111,787, all of this having been done without any expense to the country. As regards settlement with financial assistance under what is called the tripartite agreement the relief settlement from June 1, 1932, to December 31, 1934 plan, 3,948 families or 20,657 individuals were placed on the land. This, with the total which I gave a moment ago, makes a grand total of 132,444 persons, a notable achievement. The disequilibrium which is the cause of so much difficulty at the present time, manifested through unemployment and the ills that are incident to inactivity, the dissatisfaction and the festering discontent in the large cities, can be remedied to a great extent by a further prosecution of this back to the land program. I do not profess that everyone is suited to become a farmer on a large scale, but if a survey were made of the six or eight large centres of the dominion, many heads of families would be found who would be suited to take up land in the unorganized districts, and a large number would be suited to take up small holdings in organized districts. With a small amount of assistance
great and permanent relief to this ill could I believe be found. If it be true that gainful industrial employment will not in the immediate future be available to the half million unemployed, any temporary expedient which gives them a dole or a certain amount of employment on public works which are more or less necessary, is a plan which does not commend itself to my judgment. Such a policy but "skins and films the ulcerous place" which it can neither probe nor heal; it does not cut out the sore; it does not make for cure, whereas if families are reestablished on the land where they can provide for themselves, they cease to be a burden to the state and a problem to the centre in which they live.
On several occasions I have spoken in similar terms in the house and have exposed myself to the jeers of some hon. members who sit opposite. One invited me to make an attempt at farming myself, and another made some scathing remarks as to the manner of life which people lead on the land. I do not take these jeers too seriously; debate in this, as in other deliberative assemblies is conducted in that way. But I do suggest that when people are unable to provide for themselves, when for months and years they have been sustained by others, they should not be too critical of the means and opportunities offered them to become again self sustaining. I thoroughly believe that the vast majority of those who are out of work are anxious to get back to work, but I think we should also recall that throughout the ages people have not been able to escape entirely from trial and tribulation, whether they lived in Canada or elsewhere. There are things which are essential to life; they are bread, clothing, and, in countries like this, fuel; and when people have been given the opportunity to secure these they have attained quite as much as the bulk of humanity have ever been able to enjoy as far back as the records of the human family run. So I am not too much disturbed by the criticism of those who say that all should be entitled to a livelihood on a very high plane. We have cherished a delusion of that kind for a few years back; we are now paying the penalty of having been deluded.
We are approaching the spring of the year;
I suggest that it would be most beneficial if we could at the time further accelerate the land settlement undertakings of the Department of Labour. I believe that if a careful survey were made it would be found that a very substantial proportion of those who are out of work and who are suited
1256	COMMONS
Unemployment Rcliej-Mr. Hackett
to take up life on the land would be glad of that opportunity. I wish to make it quite clear that I do not advocate that all be sent off to the hinterland, merely to drown their cries of distress in an engulfing wilderness. But I do believe that with a measure of assistance a substantial number of unemployed could be placed where they would be able to make their own livelihood and regain that self respect which comes from independence.
We have heard a great deal about housing, We have heard a great deal about slums, and it has been suggested that we should devote large sums of money to tearing down buildings in the cities and replacing them with modern dwellings. I suggest that substantial sums be used to build modest homes for those who are suited to go on the land, to build those homes, or some of them at least, in districts already settled, where there are churches, schools, telephones and highways. By doing this we shall enable those who for so long have been dependent to become again self-sustaining. This would not be extremely expensive at the present time. There are few farmers in the east who are not overburdened with land, on which they find it difficult to pay the taxes, and large numbers of small farms of a few acres each could be purchased in almost any of the eastern townships, and people adapted to life on the land taken from the cities and established on them.
I hope that the hon. gentleman who introduced this amendment will realize that he has overlooked this very valuable piece of work which has been done during the past four or five years and in his reply will give the encouragement of his support to its acceleration and encourage it later by his voice and vote.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hope the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Hackett) will excuse me if I do not spend any time dealing with the matter which has engaged his attention, as I cannot imagine anything being further from the actual problems of Canada than the question which he has been discussing.
I think the matter of human suffering, which has become so widespread in Canada and in the civilized world, owing to our inability to use the goods which we are able to produce, is well worthy of the time which this house has so far spent in this discussion. I think we are indebted to the hon. member who by his amendment brought to the attention of the house and the country this major problem of our time. Of course the amend-

ment moved by the hon. member for Van-couvei Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) is in effect one of want of confidence. He bases his no confidence motion on the fact that the government has failed to solve the problem of unemployment. If failure to solve the problem of unemployment merits a vote of no confidence I am surely going to vote for this amendment. I shall do so for the same reason that I voted no confidence in the government preceding this one, when the party to which my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre gives his allegiance was in power. We moved a similar resolution to this for a similar reason, that that government had failed to solve the problem of unemployment. In fact I imagine that such a motion would be applicable to any government in the world at present, with the possible exception of Russia. So I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver Centre in that respect.
I agree with him also in another respect; he said the other day that the government had sown the wind and was reaping the whirlwind. As I looked at my hon. friend when he said that I could easily agree with him that they were certainly reaping the whirlwind, for there was no lack of either whirl or wind.
But of course unemployment is not a new problem; we have been discussing it ever since I came to this house. It is true that the problem is getting more acute, but the causes of unemployment during the nine years of Liberal rule were exactly the same as they are now. It is true that there were not so many unemployed, but it is also true that those who were unemployed had the same right to be employed as the greater number have to-day. Time and time again I, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and others of this group brought the unemployment question to the attention of that government, as we have done with this government, so I say the problem is not new but is only growing more acute. The efficiency of machine production determines the size of the unemployed army. Poverty keeps pace with our progress day by day. However much we may deplore the lack of action on the part of this and other governments in years gone by in dealing with the unemployment question, a neurotic haste in doing wrong things at the eleventh hour will not make matters very much better, and I would say that the proposals of the hon. member who moved this resolution, with which I will deal later, are proposals made in neurotic haste to do wrong things.
The debate so far has not dealt at all with the economic question which is the problem of the modern world to-day. I think I could

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Irvine
sum up the entire debate, so far as the two major parties are concerned, by saying that the Liberal party has demonstrated beyond doubt that the Conservative party has failed to solve the problem of unemployment, and I think the Conservative party has demonstrated with equal thoroughness that the Liberal party did not solve it when it had the chance and do not know how to solve it now. I think I agree entirely with both sides; I think we can make it unanimous. Each has proved that the other could not meet the problem. So I am glad of this debate if for no other reason than that it affords most excellent propaganda for the C.C.F. That is what I have been trying to prove for a long time, and now these two parties have helped me out by proving it themselves, so that is something we will not have to do over again. Any person reading the debate on this, as on other motions, and seeing how effectively and completely the one party has proved the inability of the other, surely cannot have very much faith in either.
The hon. member who moved this motion apparently holds the view that if the Liberal party were in power it would be better for the unemployed, that the Liberals would be able to carry on in a better and more effective way than the present government have done. That may very well be, but I would ask on what grounds the hon. gentleman expects the members of this house or the people of Canada to believe him. First there is the ground of past experience and past history. It is an unfortunate thing that history should come up thus to meet us on the very threshold of a great ambition, but it does, and the history of the Liberal party-with which I need spend no time because, as I say that has been dealt with very well by the Conservative party-during the nine years it was in office here shows that it was just as helpless to meet the unemployment situation as the present government was or is. We moved similar motions time and time again. I recall that the last one we moved was in the last session during which the Liberal party held power. We did all we could to impress the Prime Minister of that day with the fact that there was unemployment in Canada, but I recall that he spent a good deal of time in trying to prove to us that there could not be unemployment in Canada because during that year Canada produced more goods than during any other year in all her history. Therefore he argued that there could not be unemployment in Canada. Everyone knows that the figures he gave were accurate, and that because they were true there was unemployment, for what
makes unemployment but producing more goods than you ever did before? On that occasion, sir, I did my best to put the government out of power because they had no policy with regard to unemployment. I shall do the same with regard to the present motion and the present government and for the very same reason, that neither party has done anything at all to meet the economic condition from which unemployment comes.
So with regard to the past there is no good reason why we should believe that the party of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) would do any more with regard to unemployment than the present government have done. My second reason, however, is that even in his proposals he speaks only for himself; he is not speaking for his party, and he makes that very clear. I have very great respect for the personal opinions of my hon. friend. I am always glad to hear them; they are fresh from the anvil of his own hammering, they are sincere and they are vigorously expressed. But after all they are only his opinions and really they have no more value than my opinions, nor does it mean that the Liberal party will stand by his opinions any more than they will stand by mine. So from that point of view also there is no reason to suppose that his party would do any better than the other party.
The next reason for lack of faith in his proposals is the proposals themselves. The views expressed by him, however commendable they might be in themselves, have absolutely no bearing upon the main issue now before the people of Canada. I will refer briefly to some of his arguments, and first I should like to refer to what he regards as the causes. I want to state emphatically that in my opinion he is entirely wrong with respect to what he regards as causes; in fact not one of the causes that he mentions is a cause of anything at all. They are results and effects, not causes at all. First he says there are the unemployable. The unemployable are not a cause; they are the result of something else. Next he speaks of rapidly changing adjustments, and I suppose he means the necessity for rapidly changing adjustments, which we have failed to make. He says that is another cause of unemployment, or in other words he has very properly said that unemployment is a cause of unemployment, however that may sound. Then he says that the codes of many organizations in Canada to-day, as in other nations, make it almost impossible	to
provide gainful occupation for many of
1258	COMMONS
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Irvine
our youth. That, he says, is another cause. That is the problem itself; that is not a cause. Next he says that business cycles of unemployment are inevitable. Is that a cause of anything? Is it even good sense to make the statement? It may be very true; it is true that these cycles have been recurring over certain periods of history, but to say that they are inevitable, that they must keep on, is to say that we are incapable of dealing wtih the economic problem which produces those cycles.
So these are not causes at all, and since my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre has not found the cause it will not be surprising if he fails to find the remedy. Then he proceeds further to indicate that laissez-faire spirit in which he was born and bred, in which he has grown up and which he still serves most faithfully. I want to quote that section because I believe it bespeaks his political impotence:
Business itself must be willing to outlaw those forms of competition which are socially destructive.
That is the abracadabra of politics so far as the hon. member is concerned. He says business ought to do that, "And so, please, Mr. Business, kindly please the hon. member for Vancouver Centre; get busy and do it." That is the spirit behind the statement I have read.
But notice further: He indicates he wants to get rid of the fruits of competition without getting rid of competition itself; he seeks to do something which is impossible. So far as the evils of competition are concerned the hon. member stands with hon. members in this comer of the chamber, but he parts with us when he says, "These evils we hope big business will smooth out, but we will keep competition." That is a most impossible position to take. And so he states that "business itself must be willing to outlaw those forms of competition which are socially destructive, and it must give due shares to labour, the consumer, to management and to capital." Again we must leave it to the moral sense of big business and soulless corporations to do the fair thing with labour and the community. Of course that is the spirit and soul of Industry and Humanity-a very excellent book, the only difficulty with it being that no person ever thought of attempting to follow the suggestions contained in it, and if he did make such an attempt I am afraid he would not go very far.
Then the hon. member continues:
It must be content with business profits-[DOT]
That is, big business.
(Mr. Irvine.)
-and must not search unduly after illusory and unsocial speculative gains.
In other words the corporations must be good little fellows, go to Sunday school, do all the things we ask, and we will allow them to proceed. He states:
It must be willing to endure that minimum of government control which the general interest requires. In short, shall I say, there must be a new partnership between business and politics in Canada for the sake of the common man.
What a glorious and pious wish that is! Then,
Governments need the assistance of constructive and productive business, and I think business needs the guidance and cooperation of governments, not bludgeoning, not dragooning, not conscripting, but in a real alliance responsive to the promotings of the social conscience.
So that we are not to force anything; we are not to have any law which would compel these people to do the right thing. We are just to ask them nicely to do it; we are not to dragoon them, but must leave them to the social conscience. But a corporation neither has nor can be affected by a conscience.
That is the second hopeless feature of the proposals offered by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre. We turn next to his personal proposals. These are many in number; I believe he strained to reach fourteen, but scarcely made it. I imagine the effectiveness of these proposals must be judged in inverse ratio to their numerical strength. Let us go over some of them. First he states he is giving only his personal views. Then he said:
I sugest that we should have immediately at our disposal a complete census and registration of those now unemployed.
Well, there is no cure for unemployment in a census, that I know of. For a long time we have been taking the census of the unemployed and yet we have made no progress. Indeed the hon. member quoted figures which I presume were fairly accurate, but the fact that he had those figures did not help the unemployed. However, he states that if we have those figures we will proceed to find how many are unemployable, and that when we have found the number we must find some special measures for their care. Precisely, Mr. Speaker; that is begging the question. What are the special measures for their care which the hon. member for Vancouver Centre had in mind? That is the point. We have to take his word that he will provide special measures, but we do not know what they are or how he will provide them.

Unemployment Reliej-Mr. Irvine
Next he states:
I want to advocate the handling of this entire problem as one of national emergency.
Again that would not help unemployment. Every problem of a social nature is more or less of a national emergency. Then he states:
I advocate the undertaking by the government of public works on a limited scale in which the greater proportion of the appropriation shall go to labour rather than to supplies or equipment.
He does not indicate how the greater proportion is to go to these people who do the work. May I point out to the hon. member that the only way the government could carry out the works suggested under his proposal would be to go further into debt. When the hon. member had completed his public works the unemployment situation would not be improved, and he would not have touched the problem at all. Then he states:
I advocate cooperation with the construction industry and other business for privately directed works and undertakings, their financing to be assisted by the government, which shall be completely reimbursed for any advances made.
That is to say, he proposes that to give people work the government shall finance private institutions' making private profits. Already we have more of the goods which those people would be engaged in producing than we know what to do with. Yet that is one of the cures he suggests for unemployment. Next:
I suggest adequate, immediate and effective measures to increase our domestic and foreign trade.
The proper answer to that is, "Oh, yeah?" But these "adequate, immediate and effective measures" have no existence, not even in the imagination of the hon. member-and he has lots of that. They have no existence; no person has proposed them, and in the second place there is no foreign trade to be got, no matter how much he may plan to get it. He goes on:
I suggest the reduction of rates of interest on all outstanding obligations in the Dominion of Canada.
That is a suggestion of which I approve, but certainly it has nothing to do with the unemployment situation. I would go farther than my hon. friend; I would not only reduce it, I would wipe it out entirely. It will have to be wiped out and it ought to be wiped out. There is no justification for its being maintained. Why should it be two per cent, why three per cent, why any per cent? If we can justify one we can justify the other.
But the suggestion of the hon. member has nothing to do with unemployment. Then:
I suggest a national conversion scheme reducing the interest on all internal debt to two and a half per cent.
Again I would have no objection to reducing the interest; I would prefer to wipe it out entirely, but that would not employ our people. Next:
I advocate immediate negotiations with outside nations where our external bonds are held, for a mutually satisfactory scheme for the reduction of interest on external bonds.
Again I have no objection to his going cap in hand to those outside of Canada to whom we owe money and pleading with them to reduce our interest rates. Although I have no objection to it, I do not think we would get very far by doing so. Then:
I suggest the increase of our currency by $430,(KK),000, which is scientifically justifiable by the appreciation of gold values.
Just notice that,-"scientifically," if you please. He uses the expression "scientifically justifiable." May I point out to my hon. friend that if we did that, then perhaps next year we should have to kill the $430,000,000 because of the depreciation of gold, and we would be just as unscientific in the one case as we were in the other. I would ask my hon. friend to please not charge up to science the superstition to which he adheres. There is no man who can talk of a scientific monetary system that deals with gold or the gold basis, and I hope my hon. friend will keep that in mind.
But here is the point, Mr. Speaker. What is he going to create this $430,000,000 for? He is going to create at to pay the bondholders of Canada for fear they might lose something. He is going to pay the debts of Canada with $430,000,000 of credit supplied on a scientific gold basis. I do not give a curse for the bondholders of Canada at the moment. I am not going to create $430,000,000 to pay them. I want $430,000,000, if that is enough, to go into the pockets of the people of Canada to buy goods, but as soon as you pay $430,000,000 of debt you have cancelled $430,000,000 of purchasing power. There is the economics of my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre. That is his proposal, and perhaps it is just as well that it was his personal viewpoint only, and that he was not speaking for the Liberal party.
Now I turn to some other proposals which he made. He wants to balance the budget. I am not interested in that. That is a bankers' policy. Next he says:
For the permanently unemployable I suggest the extension of the principle of the War Veterans' Allowance Act.
1260	COMMONS
Unemployment Relief-Mr. Irvine
I have no objection to extending that to everybody in Canada, so far as I am concerned. He also said:
For the partially unemployable I suggest physical reestablishment for a limited period and land settlement on small holdings.
Now what does that mean-physical reestablishment for a limited period? And then, mind you, land settlement. I wonder why he did not get into cooperation with the hon. member who preceded me in this debate (Mr. Hackett). Anyone who starts out with a policy of land settlement at the present moment I think had better not be replied to at all. I think that is the best way to treat that argument. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre went on:
Such then, Mr. Speaker, is the problem and such are some of the suggested remedies.
Now, Mr. Speaker, with all due respect to my hon. friend I desire to emphasize that he never even got in touch with the problem in his whole speech and he did not have a single solution in the whole twelve or fourteen or sixteen, or whatever it was, points that he put forward. I know that the government has not got a solution either, but I am centering my attention on the man who moved the motion because he thought he had something, and I want to find out whether he does have something or not.
I know that the government has not a solution for this problem so far. It may have one in its mind but it has not proposed it, and
so I am centering my attention on the proposal that is before the house. And such are the proposals that the Liberal party spokesman, although he was not speaking for the Liberal party, asks us to consider in connection with the unemployment problem. I might put it all in a word and say that my hon. friend is trying to patch capitalism, and that, of course, is what the government is trying to do. My hon. friend proposes to patch it m a netw place. He is proposing a patch of a different colour and of a different size, but apart from that there is no difference between his patch and the patch of the government except that perhaps, after all, the patches of the government would be more effective than the ones he is proposing to put on.

speechtext: On which part?

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Modestly forbids me to tell you exactly where they would be. So far as I am concerned, and I think that in this I am speaking as well for my group here, we do not believe that the system can be patched

effectively or in such a way that it can serve adequately. I do not hold that as a mere belief. I would be prepared, if I had the time, to bring the facts and the arguments also.
I waht now, in order to keep within the time limit at my disposal, to summarize some of the reasons why we believe that capitalism cannot be made to work effectively no matter who is trying to do it. And I still wait, as I have waited many years here, for any man on either side of the house to say how it can be made to work. I still throw that challenge to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre. If he is going to patch this system to work successfully he will have to meet the debt situation, both private, national and international, and there is no proposal today from anybody that will adequately pay the debts either of the individual or of the nation or international debts. Even if they could pay them, if they carried on with the present system it would 'be only a few months before they would have the debts duplicated because there is no private undertaking, there is no corporation undertaking, there is no public service or public work that can be undertaken until there is first a debt created to make the undertaking possible, and if the debt-creating system is 'carried on, as the hon. member for Vancouver Centre presupposes in his patching, then even if he could pay the debts, they would be back on his shoulders again in a very short time. But he not only does not propose to do away with the debt-creating system; he does not even know how to pay the debts that are already there.
Next he deals or tries to deal with a method of putting more people to work. I do not want to put more people to work just for the sake of putting more people to work. The only way we can put more people to work in Canada to-day is by putting more debts on the backs of the people. Under the present system or under the proposals of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, and also under the proposals of the government, if you could put people to work it would simply mean more unpayable, impossible debts put upon the backs of all the rest of the people of this country. Now until my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre or some hon. gentleman representing the government can tell us how they can put the people to work without creating debts can we regard either party as fit to carry on government? They cannot make capitalism work because it has gone as far as it can under its debt-creating character.

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Irvine
Next capitalism cannot go on without markets. People will not keep on producing goods unless they can sell them at a profit. Will the hon. member for Vancouver Centre or anyone on the government 'benches tell the house how they propose to get more markets for Canada. I want the hon. gentlemen to tell me in what country-let them be specific for once-we can find a market, and for what shall we find a market in that country, and for how much of that will we find a market in that country, and for how long will we have that market, and finally what will that country take from us in exchange for that which we want to get from that country? These are matters of data. Where are these markets? It is all very well to talk of wider and freer markets, of adequate methods of extending our foreign trade and all that sort of rhetoric, but where are we going to extend it? What are the goods to be sold? How much will those other countries take from us? Those are the questions which the hon. gentleman failed to answer.
Let me say next that there is no unemployment problem at all. I know that that will sound to some just as foolish as it sounded fourteen years ago when I said from this same seat that we should not go back on the gold basis but that we should reorganize the financial structure of Canada, and that we should forthwith manage and control our currency and credit in relation to the economic demands of the state. I can hear yet the jeers of the cabinet of that day.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that there is no unemployment problem. Unemployment, which should be leisure, is the boon which has come to this age as a heritage from the past. It has been made safe to us by the combination of human intelligence and ingenuity and mechanical skill, combined with the use of solar power in the production of the necessities and comforts of human life. The more of these machines we use and the -more solar energy we employ to drive them the more leisure the people have. And then we say that we have a problem of unemployment. What we have is a problem of vast social stupidity; That is our real problem.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: SUPPLY-UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You can "oh, oh" just as
much as you like, but I will let that statement stand on Hansard to speak for itself twenty-five years from now or fifty years if it takes you that long to discover that we have no unemployment problem. Unemployment should be a boon. Our real problem is to make the fullest use of all the
means of wealth production at our disposal and to distribute the products to the people. Why not spend a couple of days discussing that question? Why not get to the heart of the real problem? I do not care who has failed to solve it; I do not care whether the mistakes of the Conservative party are more or less than the mistakes of the Liberal party; I am not even interested in talking about unemployment. What I want to discuss is the question of using the idle plant equipment of Canada and the great, the vast natural resources of the country so that we may produce more goods for the people and, finally, the distribution of those goods so that the people may use them. For who is insane enough to advocate production unless what is produced is consumed by the people? And surely that is the point where our system is breaking down.
Now what is the best way of distributing goods? By wages, as we have been doing in the past? Well, wages can distribute with some efficiency while there is a scarcity of goods, but never with complete efficiency. Shall we continue trying to distribute the production of machines and solar power, production in such abundance as we know is possible, by the wage system, or shall we turn from the wage system or augment that system by a meagre, begrudged national charity? That is the only other proposal that has so far been put into action. Or shall we rather seek to distribute this abundant production by means of social dividends based on the national capacity to produce the things of life? If people have the money goods will be distributed. The chief way which the working classes have of getting money is by working for wages, but at no time have they received sufficient wages to enable them to buy back the products of their labour; and as time went on and machines displaced men and produced in greater abundance it was found that men could be dispensed with, so that they no longer had any jobs at all and therefore no purchasing power, and consequently there were huge supplies of goods that had to be burned or otherwise destroyed from time to time by corporations or by government intervention.
Primarily our problem is one of distribution, and distribution is a question primarily of finance. How can this country get money into the pockets of the consuming public? I should like to hear that question discussed. Well, we must have the right to create money as required for the distribution of goods, and that means that we must take that power out of the hands of private individuals

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Irvine
and utilize the social credit of the state in the interests of the people. My hon. friend from Vancouver Centre is willing to create
8430.000. 000.	But why $430,000,000? He proposes that sum because he says he is scientific and wants to refer it to a gold basis. But why a gold basis? Let me invite the attention of the hon. gentleman to a far more sensible and far more scientific basis than that for the issuance of supplies of money. I would invite him to consider the fact that the assets of Canada are plant, equipment and natural resources, and that these assets are estimated at $30,000,000,000, whereas the annual output of wealth is about
56.000. 000.000. Now that is a much better basis for the issuance of credit and currency than the antiquated, superstitious gold basis by which he is prepared to limit the issue of credit.
The first basis of such social dividends as I suggest is this. The great proportion of our increased production to-day is due to association and organization, so that much of the wealth produced is not traceable to any effort of any individual but rather to the social, communal efforts of all together. That is the first basis. The next basis of modem wealth production is really a heritage from all the past in mechanical ideas and in discovery and invention, as well as in organization. All these factors have made it possible for us to produce in greater abundance, but all these came to us from millions of people in the past; and these factors cannot be mastered or controlled by any one individual or corporation. We cannot allow that; they are not for sale and they must not be bought, no matter how much money any man has to buy them. These facilities of production, representing the genius of the race, are the heritage of this age; they are responsible for our increased wealth. And on that almost inexhaustible source we have a right to draw for the man who has been put out of a job by the machine, and to see to it that the goods which the machine that took his job produces shall be vouchsafed to him as a means of livelihood.
That is our problem, and there is no proposal, either from the government or from my hon. friend who moved this motion, that solves that problem. I do not suppose that any proposal of mine in this connection would be immediately and unanimously passed by this house. I will not now propose the complete financial reform which I think is necessary, but I do suggest that we make a beginning, and for once our beginning should
be constructively at the point of finance. I suggest that we begin by putting our machinery and solar power to work to produce everything we need. If we do not need things we will not produce them, and if they are already produced we will use them. But with these machines we should build homes in the most modern fashion, and all our social institutions, hospitals, schools, colleges, universities, roadls, bridges, crossings and highways. Let us enter upon a program of protection of our forests for future generations. Let us develop our vast coal fields for power and let us harness the water powers of the country so that we may bring every agency of modem civilization within the reach of the population living within the confines o>f Canada. That is a task which will put a good many people to work for a while, and after that is done they can lie back in leisure and enjoy watching the machine doing it for them. But that is our task, and the only means of accomplishing it is to employ the social credit of the nation and to utilize it, in its financial expression, to enable the people to buy back the goods they have already created and which are lying on the shelves of the warehouses or being destroyed because people are unable at present to use them. Put the money to that use and we shall soon find it necessary to produce1 more goods. Let us make that beginning by the proper use of the national credit and by giving social dividends to our people.
And through social dividends let our people have pensions starting, if you like, at the age of fifty-five, so that people of that age and over may vacate the production field and thus make room for the oncoming youth who will take their places in the workshops of Canada.

The hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) will not, I hope, be offended if I do not immediately follow his arguments. I would like first to express my amazement at the caprioles and volte faces of hon. gentlemen opposite on the question of social legislation. The day before yesterday when we were about to move to go into committee of supply to vote moneys part of which would tend to relieve unemployment, the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) immediately rose and proposed a motion which might be summed up as follows: you want to vote money. We say no because we want to declare -before you do so that you are not doing anything to relieve unemployment.

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Oagnon
May I say at the outset that I have a great admiration for the talents and eloquence of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre. Comparisons are certainly almost always bad because they lack the element which makes for perfection, but I hope my hon. friend will not be offended if I compare him to a promising apple tree matured and flourishing under the benevolent rays of the Vancouver Sun. I am afraid that my hon. friend, even if he is later entrusted with the noble task of salvaging the Liberal party from the valley of humiliation will never succeed in providing the electors of Canada with the golden apples of the Hesperides, because at the present time I am sure the house will realize that no Liberal Hercules can kill the dragon whose hundred heads are the numerous broken pledges of the Liberal platform of 1919.
Although I very much admire the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, may I express wonderment that instead of criticizing the government and finding fault with our efforts toward bringing into effect social legislation, he does not come to the rescue of Mayor McGeer and Premier Pattullo in order to salvage the financial situation of his province. Last year we had very interesting debates before the banking and commerce committee and the hon. member for Vancouver Centre brought from the sunny coast of British Columbia a new financial prodigy who was supposed to give us a panacea which would cure all our social and financial evils. For two long days we heard Mayor McGeer indulge in the wildest theories of state currency inflation. Of course nobody but himself could go into the vast depths of financial science and understand his theories. The only compliment I might pay to Mayor McGeer is that his theories were less proposterous and more understandable than those of Major Douglas which may give much joy to the Ottawa Citizen but which nevertheless cannot be understood by any Canadian citizen who has ordinary common sense.
What has been the effect of the theories of Mayor McGeer? He has been elected mayor of the great city of Vancouver and he has attempted to solve the question of the interest due on the bonds of that city. The other day we found the London newspapers stating that due to his attitude, due to his wild theories, the values of all the bonds of the cities of western Canada were declining on the markets of the world. I wonder whether our friends the Liberals will provide some saner theories after they have come out of the great banquet
the newspapers this morning have announced our friends are going to give to their leader some time in the month of March.

speechtext:
We know very well what will take place at the next election. Not only will the conscription issue be revived but we shall hear a new revival of the constitutional issue. We shall hear again the cry of conscription, and we Conservative members will be slandered and attacked and represented to the people as the wreckers of the constitution, while the Liberal party will pose as the champions of the rights of the provinces and the protectors of the constitution. Let us study for a moment what took place just a fortnight ago when the government was bringing in the unemployment insurance measure. What did

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Gagnon
we hear? We heard the former Minister of , Justice ridicule that measure, calling it a sop to the discontented. He closed his speech with a violent attack on the government, comparing the ministers to a lynching mob. These are the compliments we receive from hon. gentlemen opposite for enacting the very measures that they proposed in 1919 but had not the courage to put on the statute books when they assumed power. If it is true that such measures as those providing for social insurance, the eight hour day, the forty-eight hour week are ultra vires of the dominion parliament; if it is true that they are unconstitutional; if it is true that the enactment of such measures by the federal parliament would be destroying the rights of the provinces, why are hon. gentlemen opposite voting for them? If it is true that these measures are unconstitutional, why do my hon. friends disregard those so-called sacred rights? Why are they forsaking them? It is amazing to see hon. gentlemen opposite descending so low that in order to get power they will vote for measures which they believe to be unconstitutional and unworthy of statesmen and patriots.
Let me for the moment refer to what has taken place in our province since 1930. In that year Premier Taschereau in the legislative assembly passed an act, chapter 14 of 20 George Y, revised statutes of Quebec, to create a commission to be called the Quebec social insurance commission. I hold in my hand a report of the Quebec social insurance commission which -was composed of some of the most eminent and illustrious citizens of that province. Let me give their names. The chairman of the commission is Edouard Mort-petit, K.C., doctor of laws of Laval, who received the diploma of political science from the Sorbonne. Paris, and who is an officer of rhe Legion of Honour. The members of the commission are the Right Reverend Georges Courchesne, Bishop of Saint-Germain-de-Rimouski, emeritus professor in the Faculty of Arts of Laval university; the Venerable Frederick George Scott. Archdeacon of Quebec and rector of St. Matthew's Church, Quebec; John T. Foster, president of the trades and labour council of Montreal and member of the Labour Congress of Canada; Gerard Tremblay, deputy minister of labour for the province of Quebec, and late secretary-general of the National Catholic Labour Unions; Alphonse Lessard, M.D., provincial director of charities and of the bureau of health; and Georges-Arthur Savoy, president of the Dominion Blank Book Company, St. Johns, Quebec.
These gentlemen were entrusted by the Quebec legislature with the task of studying all problems pertaining to social insurance. I shall quote the terms of the order in council passed by the government at Quebec:
To make as complete a survey as possible of the following questions and of the manner in which the problems which they entail may be regulated in the province of Quebec: Old age insurance; unemployment insurance; sickness insurance; disability insurance; aid to needy mothers; family placements; manner of adoption and placement of adopted children; assistance to large families; sanitary conditions of factories and of the workers in these factories; occupational illnesses; medical inspection of workmen employed in dangerous tasks; medical attention in the work shops; sanitary education of the working men; and all other problems of social insurance.
These gentlemen visited all the provinces in Canada, and went abroad. They studied the social insurance schemes in England, France, Germany and almost all countries in Europe. They delivered various reports, and the sixth report dealing with unemployment insurance was filed with the Quebec government in the last days of December, 1932.
Now, what took place just ten days after that? In the beginning of January, 1933 a great banquet was held in the city of Quebec. This was a banquet tendered by the Liberals to the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and to the former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). There, Mr. Speaker, in order to revive the failing courage of the Liberals, and because at this very banquet my former opponent in Dorchester, the former Solicitor General, had the courage to blame the Liberals for their lack of policy, the former Minister of Justice stood in his place and praised the great report which had been produced by the Quebec social insurance commission. I have before me a quotation from Le Soleil of Quebec, the issue of January 15, 1933. My translation of the report contained therein concerning the observations of the hon. member for Quebec East is as follows:
Let me congratulate now the government of the province of Quebec for the work of the social insurance commission which they have instituted, and for the report which has just been made public. It is a Liberal document. Many suggestions are therein made which I have heard called socialistic theories. I am happy now to be in the company of Bishop Courchesne and Doctor Montpetit. 'That report does honour to our province, and Liberals ought to study it and work to bring about the application of the illuminating principles which it contains.
As I have said, that speech was made on January 15, 1933, by the former Minister of Justice and in the name of the Liberal party.

In his speech he proclaimed the report of the commission to be a Liberal document. Let us see the conclusions to which the commission came, respecting sooial insurance. Did the commission state that social insurance against unemployment ought to be instituted by the provinces'- Did the commissioners make any observations against the so-called attempt of the dominion to wreck the rights of the provinces by setting afoot a scheme of insurance against unemployment? No. At page 203 of the report the commission said:
Is it possible to establish unemployment insurance on a provincial basis in a federated state such as Canada? The answer is in the affirmative, for the example of Queensland, Australia, and of certain Swiss cantons prove the possibility. However ordinary prudence suggests that unemployment insurance should be federal in character. It is very advisable to spread the social responsibilities over the whole country, for otherwise, the provinces which participate find themselves in a condition of inferiority with respect to the non-participants. It must not be forgotten that the expenses involved in social legislation should be incorporated in the net cost of production. If certain provinces do not enjoy the benefits of tariff protection, the industrialists of those provinces must of necessity aim at an equality in social obligations if they do not desire to embark on a policy of rivalry which is not only impossible to maintain, but is unfair.
The commission quoted the opinion of the railway workers of Canada who stated that there was no other conclusion to come to but that of providing a federal scheme of unemployment insurance. Do we. See the flagrancy of the contradictions of the former Minister of Justice when on January 15, 1933, he proclaimed as a Liberal document this report which recommended a federal scheme of unemployment insurance? Yet only a few days ago in this very chamber he blamed the government, and compared the ministers to a lynching mob because they have sought to effect the precise proposals and recommendations of the Quebec social insurance commission.
What did the Liberal party in Quebec do in order to set afoot the .recommendations of the commission? The commission, whose report I have before me, recommended that the Quebec government should adopt a federal system of old age pensions. They recommended, further, that the provinces should cooperate with the federal government in order to bring about the necessary measures of reform to which the Liberal party had pledged itself at the convention of 1919. What was done by Liberals? Nothing,-nothing has been done.

When, in the month of March 1933 we were fighting in this chamber to obtain from the House of Commons the power to take the necessary steps to relieve unemployment, what position was taken in the province of Quebec? What did the former Minister of Justice say in the city of Quebec on March 28, 1933? I have before me L'Evenement of Quebec, a publication sympathetic to the former Minister of Justice. It indicates that he at that time compared Mr. Bennett to Hitler, a man who in some countries has been called a gangster and a murderer. That will give some idea of the way hon. gentlemen opposite discuss political questions in Quebec.
Would hon.. members like to have some idea of the way hon. gentlemen opposite are trying to bring about unity among the Canadian people? Let us see what he said on March 28, 1933, when he was speaking against the payment of moneys which this government has voted in order to help the provinces of Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta. Here is what he said:
Shall we take the money of the province of Quebec to maintain Mr. Anderson in power? Is it not too much of a sardonic irony?
That is the way hon. gentlemen opposite are trying to effect unity among the Canadian people and bring about a closer understanding between the races in Canada. Speaking at Trois Pistoles on July 17, 1933, the former Minister of Justice reiterated the same principles. He condemned the government, and described as an international comedy the London conference which was being held at the time, and at whieh our Prime Minister was taking a worthy stand, one which received the general approval of statesmen throughout the world. The hon. gentleman proclaimed himself a .champion of reforms and said "I am not going to the right. I am not going to the left. I am going forward."

speechtext:
I am pleased to hear hon. gentlemen apposite applaud that statement, Mr. Speaker, but it is surprising that these gentlemen who claim to go forward should take every opportunity to block our legislation and denounce it as being unconstitutional and ultra vires and so on.
This is not all, Mr. Speaker; this little story has many chapters which are very interesting to the people of Quebec and the people of Canada at large. What has taken place in the province of Quebec? Not only have we seen the Conservative opposition in that province call for reforms which will tend

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Gagnon
to promote the welfare of all classes, but we have seen a secession in the Liberal ranks; we have a new wing of the Liberal party in Quebec headed by Mr. Paul Gouin, the son of the former Minister of Justice, and supported by a distinguished member of this house, the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Lacroix). This Liberal wing, which is growing stronger and stronger every day, is calling for reforms also, and is asking that the province of Quebec set its seal of approval on the reforms we are putting on the statute books. What is the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) doing, he who calls himself the man who goes forward? He does not do anything, as he did nothing when he was in power from 1021 to 1930. While the hon. member for Beauce, Mr. Paul Gouin and others are denouncing Mr. Tasohereau and the terrible dictatorship which is enslaving the province of Quebec, through you, Mr. Speaker, I ask the hon. member for Quebec East to tell the people of Canada and particularly the people of Quebec whether he is for Tasohereau and against Gouin and Lacroix or for Lacroix and Gouin and against Tas-chereau with regard to social legislation.
We Conservatives are not afraid to speak about our constitution, because we have preserved and maintained the confederation pact. It is strange, when the Conservative party is bringing about reforms which are demanded by public opinion throughout Canada, to find that the Liberal party stands up and says: "Stop; you are going to encroach on the rights of the provinces." Then we hear Senator Lemieux and Senator Dandurand say in the .Senate. "We must respect the covenant; this is a sacred pact. You must not touch it: it is a wonderful work." In other circumstances, when a racial issue arises we hear the same gentlemen say that the fathers of confederation, because they were Conservatives, did not take the necessary steps to protect the minorities in Canada. These are the flagrant contradictions we find in the Liberal party. Even now we hear the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) attack the fathers of confederation in the maritime provinces, while on the other hand the leader of the Liberal party in the Senate and Senator Lemieux pose as champions of the constitution. I for one would be very much afraid to touch the .sections of the confederation pact which deal with the rights of minorities, because those rights are sacred to my race. The Conservatives have always maintained the constitution, and we are going to preserve intact the rights of minorities in Canada.
I respectfully submit, Mr. Speaker, that it is very dangerous to make constitutional issues of purely economic problems. You cannot ignore the overwhelming trend of public opinion throughout Canada at the present time which calls for social reforms. Is there a financier, a statesman, an economist or an ordinary layman endowed with common sense who will pretend that if we enact a social insurance scheme we are endangering the constitution or encroaching on the rights of the provinces? Why, we are protecting the exchequer of the provinces, because we are assuming the whole of that social legislation cost which is denounced by hon. gentlemen opposite as being too great. Why should the provinces complain if we establish a social insurance policy which will not cost the provinces anything? Why should the provinces object if we assume the whole cost of old age pensions; why should the provinces object if we relieve unemployment by establishing the eight hour day and forty-eight hour week, establish minimum wages and take the necessary steps to curb and destroy the monopolies and mergers which took place during the Liberal regime from 1921 to 1930? Hon. gentlemen opposite ought to be afraid to invite these party quibbles and this political strife in this way, because the consumers of Canada have suffered too much since confederation through some useless and fruitless battles which have been waged between the provinces and the dominion. Take for instance the fisheries case which was discussed the other day in the committee on the British North America Act by the hon. member for Gloucester and myself. That litigation began in 1882 and did not come to an end until 1919 or thereabouts. The situation has been made worse, because the maritime fisheries of Quebec have been illegally and unconstitutionally transferred to the province of Quebec, though the maritime fisheries in great part belong to the crown in the right of the dominion. At the present time we have legislation which is going to save agriculture; I refer to the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. Do we see that legislation attacked in Ontario, in the maritimes or in western 'Canada? No; we see it attacked on constitutional grounds only in the province of Quebec, and the person attacking it there is encouraged by the Liberal party of that province. That is not all, Mr. Speaker. On the 23rd of March there will be a banquet at Quebec city to commemorate the great legal battles which have been waged between the provinces and the dominion since 1867. I hope the gentlemen who attend that

banquet will not forget the loss of Labrador and the loss of that part of our national heritage.
I believe I have only one minute of my time remaining, Mr. Speaker, and in that minute I should like to recall the stirring appeal made to hon. members of this house last year by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) whom I should like to see returned by acclamation at the next election. The hon. gentleman urged political parties to forget party strife and to cooperate in order to bring about necessary measures of reform. I should like to urge hon. gentlemen opposite to read what he said, and may I express the hope that some George Brown will arise on the other side and help the government in order to cooperate in bringing about social justice and the dawn of a new era of happiness and prosperity.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the viewpoint of this corner of the house has been put forward often enough in this debate. I believe four members out of a possible fifteen have taken part in this discussion, and if it were not for the fact that the viewpoint put forward by all four is quite contrary to my opinion I should not have taken any part in this discussion. All of those who have preceded me from this corner have stated very definitely that they are going to support the amendment. I am forced to state just as definitely that I am going to oppose the amendment, and therefore I feel like giving in a few minutes a few reasons why I propose to do so.
The motion before the house has been moved by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) to the effect that the house go into committee of supply, and the matter which we are now debating is an amendment thereto proposed by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie). I shall not read the amendment because all who are in the chamber are acquainted with its contents.
Since I came to this house a number of years ago I have felt non-partisan, and I still do. As an independent member I have felt obliged to decide which of the major parties I should support in this house, and I think that is true of all the independent members here. For some nine years we supported a Liberal government, and for the past five years we have been supporting the present government. At the present time it is incumbent upon us to decide whether we shall support this amendment or not.

I have been led to ask myself what would be the effect of this amendment if it were carried, and I credit the hon. member who moved it with sincerity enough to wish to see it carried. I think he put it forward in the hope that it would be accepted by the house. Now if it is carried by a majority vote and accepted by the house, what would be the effect of that? The effect of that would be the immediate resignation of the government. I think that goes without saying. The government would not dare to carry on any longer should this amendment be carried.
That opens up another avenue of thought. If the government should forthwith resign we have quite a pretentious legislative program before us which would also go by the board. We have, for instance, Bill No. 8, which is now in the committee stage. It has received its first and second readings, and by the way on second reading it was supported unanimously by a vote of 101 to nothing. All parties in all parts of the house supported the principle of unemployment insurance. But if the amendment now before the house should be carried, it would mean that the unemployment insurance measure would have to be dropped. It is in the committee stage now and it would stay there. It would become null and void, a dead issue. I doubt if the members in this comer of the house are prepared to go that far arid say that they want that measure dispensed with entirely. It is true that some here are not in unanimous accord with some of the provisions of the bill, yet I think from the vote that was taken on the second reading we are all in favour of adopting an unemployment insurance measure in the hope that in the future it will be of some benefit to this country. Well, that measure would lapse if this amendment should carry.
We have also on the order paper Bill No. 15. It too is in the committee stage. It makes certain amendments to the Canadian Farm Loan Act. I am quite satisfied from having listened to the debate in this chamber on these amendments that there is perhaps not a member in this house who is opposed to them. They propose to increase the money available for agricultural purposes from $40,000,000 to $90,000,000, but should this amendment carry it means that these amendments to the farm loan act would be done away with, that that increased amount provided by the bill for taking care of farmers' debts would not be available. There is another point that I fear the members in this corner of the house are

We represent agricultural constituencies in this corner as well as other sections of the house, and I am sure we are quite anxious to see that $90,000,000 made available during this session for use under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act Here is one member who wants to see that money put where it will be available for the farmers who are trying to refund their debts at a lower rate of interest. But if we carry the amendment which is now before us there is no possibility of that money being made available during this session.
We have some other measures on the order paper. There is Bill No. 21 calling for the implementing of the eight hour day and the forty-eight hour week. Personally I would not shed any tears if that were to fall, because the voters I represent-and they are real labour people and I am a real labour representative-do not quibble at working eight hours a day or forty-eight hours a week. They are practically all farmers, and I think perhaps most of them sleep about eight hours and work the rest of the day. So as far as that measure goes it would not affect agriculturists very much, but I am surprised that the labour members have endorsed this amendment with the possible ultimate objective of defeating this eight hour day and forty-eight hour week.
There is also Bill No. 22 for a weekly day of rest in industrial undertakings. These latter two bills I have mentioned have just received their first reading. If the amendment before the house carries, these two bills are dispensed with and there is no possibility of their being carried this session.
There is one other point that is more important than any of those I have mentioned, and that is that the report of the price spreads and mass buying commission has not yet been presented to the house, and of course the legislation to be based on that report is not yet before the house. Now if there is any measure that the people of Canada are looking forward to hopefully it is the legislation that is to be based on the report of the price spreads and mass buying commission; but if we adopt this amendment it means that such a report cannot be made and that legislation based upon it will not be brought forward this session. That is thrown into the scrap heap so far as this session is concerned.
If that is what the amendment means, the dispensing of all these measures because of the resignation of the government, then what would be the result of the election that would immediately follow? That is another question that I have been led to ask myself-what 92582-81 j
would be the likely effect of an election? Well, it is possible that there might be a change of government; it is just barely possible. I would not state that as any prophecy. I know that some of our Liberal friends are quite optimistic and hopeful. Probably the wish is father to the thought that there will be a change of government, and there may be; I am not prepared to say. I have endeavoured in the past to prophesy in regard to political matters, and usually I have prophesied wrong, so I would not like to make any prophecy now as to whether or not there would be a change of government. But suppose there would be a change; what has been offered to us by the official opposition, which we are agreed would then be the government of the day? What is offered to us by this party known as the official opposition, the Liberal party of Canada? I was amused and surprised last night, listening to the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Luchkovich) lining up the Liberal party and scoring them most unmercifully because they had nothing to offer, and yet he ended by saying that he was going to vote for the amendment which would have the effect of putting out the present government and putting in its place those who, he said, had nothing to offer. I could not just travel with him all the way along the road. It became rather tortuous and I could not follow him.

speechtext:
The natural result of the tearing up of the Natural Products Marketing Act-and I am forced to conclude, 'from the attitude of the Liberal party when the act was before us, that they are not friendly to it-would be that our marketing scheme, which was voted on last week in the three prairie provinces would go by the board, and all the facilities afforded the primary producers would be dispensed with. But there is another point I would touch upon. In 1932, I believe, we passed here what became known as the Ottawa trade agreements. I fear to come to the conclusion, but I am almost forced to it, that the Liberal party are in duty bound to scrap these Ottawa trade agreements. Oh, I know they mean to scrap certain parts of them; but if certain

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Carmichael
parts of the agreements are scrapped at this end it means that the agreements fall down, because there are two parties to them and no change can be made at this end unless the other party at the other end is agreeable to such change. It follows therefore that if certain changes are made here the agreements will fall by the way, and become obsolete. Now, we had a Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act passed last session, and I am not sure of the attitude of the Liberal party towards that. Like the hon. member for St. James, they may have a change of heart either now or before they come into power, and they may not scrap it because it is a very popular piece of legislation in the prairies. But you cannot guarantee that they would not do away with that either. Unfortunately, as has been pointed out from this corner, no definite pronouncement has been made by the leader of the Liberal party. He who, according to their ideas and ambitions and hopes, is not very far removed from being Prime Minister of Canada, has made no pronouncement as to what that party proposes to do. His nine years of experience as Prime Minister and the past five years as leader of the opposition have made him discreetly wise and he is not saying anything.
The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) has moved an amendment and he has stated very definitely what "I" propose to do. He says: "What I advocate, and I am giving my personal views only, not necessarily the' views of any party or group," and he proceeds to give us twelve points. Probably they have some virtue in them, but they are the individual views of one member and do not necessarily represent the opinions of the Liberal party. So that there we are faced with the alternative of putting into power a party that has told us nothing of what it is going to do-and we know a number of things they will do which will not be beneficial. A lot of legislation that has been passed, and a good deal more that is in the act of being passed, will be prejudiced considerably toy a change of government; and yet we have before us from the Liberal party nothing official on which we can base our hopes if we support this amendment to put out the party now governing and put in the party now in opposition. The burden of the official opposition is just to put Bennett out; and the burden of the Liberal press across Canada is, "Just put the Conservatives out and let the Liberals in." That is not a very good reason for voting for the amendment now before the house.
There is considerable virtue in the amendment and1 I am not finding any fault for its being brought to the attention of the house. Its main thought is unemployment and its remedy. I doubt if I will take the time now to go into the question of unemployment to any extent except to say that I consider it worthy of being debated and I presume at some future time the house will be afforded an opportunity of discussing the question and suggesting remedies. But I do hold the view, contrary of course to that of some hon. gentlemen in this corner, that the only possible permanent solution for our unemployment problem is to get a more evenly balanced adjustment as between urban and rural populations. For the past two generations we have been educating our boys and girls away from the land which is, I was going to say their heaven-intended place to live, that is on the land, in touch with nature, working and getting their living to a large extent from the soil. For the past two generations we have been educating our people along a line that has induced them to move into the industrial centres, to enter into industrial, business and professional life and away from agricultural life. It seems to me that we must return to the basic principle of getting our population back where it belongs, namely on the land.
While many commissions have been appointed, many investigations held and even some (books written, I believe the most sensible thing for us to do in connection with this unemployment question would be to appoint a dominion land settlement commission that would have authority to make a survey in conjunction with the provinces and the smaller municipalities with a view to getting the good land lined up that would be available without cost to our boys, young men and families who are agriculturally inclined. I know in my province there is plenty of land held in some instances by the provincial government; in every township sections 11 and 29 are school lands; many of these sections have not yet been sold and some that have been sold have reverted to the crown, also in our municipalities there are scores of quarter sections that have been taken over in recent years under tax sale proceedings. Such lands might be made available without charge to those who are agriculturally inclined and under a properly set up and efficiently working commission boys, young men and families who are agriculturally inclined might thus be placed on such lands and assisted for from three to five

Unemployment Relief-Mr. Carmichael
