speechtext:
I take this first opportunity to congratulate the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hanson). With reference to that hon. gentleman may I repeat what I said about -his colleague the Minister of Finance, that I am sure he is abler than the Prime Minister, because he answers the questions that one puts to him. It is a great credit to him, and for that reason I congratulate him very heartily.
We have heard a great deal about unemployment in the last few days. The reason for unemployment is the decrease in trade, and we have a decrease in trade because tariffs have been increased. The minister is an able man; he has been sworn in as minister because of his ability. If he takes the trouble to go through the records of his department he will see that the number of unemployed has more than doubled and trebled since the tariff was increased by his leaders. Unemployment is the child of high tariffs. For this reason I urge on the hon. gentleman the same recom-

mendation I made to his colleague the Minister of Finance. Let him steal a stick of dynamite from the office of the Prime Minister-the stick that was not used to blast our way into the markets of the world-and let him blast the high tariff walls. When we look over the statistics of the Department of Trade and Commerce we are sorry to see the great decrease in trade, even following the Ottawa imperial conference of 1932. The minister knows very well-and he may answer me if he desires to do so-that our trade with the British empire last year was $29,000,000 less than it was during the last twelve months the Mackenzie King government was in power. Our domestic exports to the United Kingdom in the twelve months ending August 31, 1934, were $35,000 more than they were for the same period in 1930. I admit that. I admit that these figures are correct if you consider only domestic exports, but if you consider at the same time Canadian exports of foreign products it will be seen that our exports to the United Kingdom each year this government have been in power were less than they were in the last year the Mackenzie King government were in power.

It is not the intention to proceed further with this item at this time, and I would ask if he would be good enough to interrupt his speech now and continue it at a later date so that I might ask the committee to defer consideration of this item, which will be gone into in the ordinary way, so that another department may be brought in.

speechtext:
I will agree to any request the hon. gentleman makes in his own behalf, because when I wrote him he was very polite and courteous to me, but I strongly object to any other department being brought in for a subsidy to-day. I object to the estimates of any other department being considered, but the hon. gentleman is a new minister, and I am ready with an open heart to do anything he asks for himself. I do not know what other minister he has in mind, however, and I have my fears. I hope the hon. gentleman will not say that I am discourteous to him. I am willing to cooperate to the fullest extent so long as I know with whom I am dealing. I am dealing with the Minister of Trade and Commerce now. He knows that all the propaganda that has been published in the press with regard to the benefits of the imperial agreements is bluff and humbug, which has been published in order to satisfy the advertisers. The truth is entirely different.
Now, sir, to sum up, when the estimates

Questions
come up again it will be impossible for the hon. gentleman to deny what I am going to say, because I took the trouble to go through all the figures. Our imports from the United Kingdom are millions of dollars less than they were in 1930 and our exports to the United Kingdom-if we include the exports of foreign goods-are also less than they were in that year, though they are a little more than they were in 1932. May I say also to the hon. gentleman that the Canadian-British empire trade was $29,000,000 less. I will leave it to the minister to answer my statement. If he wishes time in which to answer me I will give it to him; there is one minute left in which he can say yes or no. The point is that it is now two and a half years since the imperial agreements were concluded. Our trade with the United Kingdom and the other countries of the empire is $29,000,000 less than it was during the twelve months ending August 31, 1930, the last year of the King administration. May I ask the minister whether or not that is true. He has time to answer yes or no.

When I first came into the house I tried to establish the status of the settlers and I was glad to hear on Monday of this week that the Minister of Labour was placing some classes of settlers under the scheme. He stated that settlers operating farms under contract with the director of soldiers' settlement could apply for the benefits of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. I believe the minister tried to answer my question last week in regard to giving the exact status of the settlers, but no final decision was reached. There is only one standard, that of colonization settlers, because you cannot build up classes within classes and you must necessarily permit all settlers, even if they are not or have not been soldiers, to come under the scheme.
I would like the committee to be fully seized of the exact situation so far as not'hern Ontario in its relation to this act is concerned and I believe the same thing applies also to northern Quebec and the newer sections of colonization of the prairie provinces and British Columbia. In the two provincial ridings of Cochrane, Ontario, there are over 3,600 families who have settled on the land and who are actual farmers in the full sense of the word although they do not own their farms outright. Their farms still belong to the crown in the right of the province. These people would not come under the scheme. Surely if it is possible for soldier settlers to come under the scheme these people who are actual settlers, living on their holdings and getting their living out of farming, ought to be able to come under the act. The minister was not definite in his answer the other day and there was no possibility of arriving at a conclusion or giving a full definition of the status of people in actual occupation. As I say, if it is possible for soldier settlers to come under this act, it should be possible also for an actual settler, one who has occupied his land for a number of years and to whom the land belongs to some extent, to come under the act. I am sincere in my pleading on behalf of that rural population. When we talk of agriculturists, we must include not only farmers who own their land but also the man whose actual occupation is farming. This should be possible within certain limits.
I fully appreciate the statement made by the Minister of Finance the other day that this was a colonization scheme. I do not want it to be taken as a colonization scheme;

Farm Loan Act
but the last stage of colonization, when a man is almost ready to get his deed, having sufficient land cleared but being unable under provincial regulations to get it, is the time that the central government should come to his help. It should be possible to bring within the provisions of this measure the real settlers in the newer sections, as well as the soldier settler. There Should be no distinction. If you are going to make classes within classes it will bring trouble. Again I make this urgent plea, and I am going to keep on making it, because it is very important. It applies just as forcibly to the riding of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) as to that I have the honour to represent. In such ridings there are thousands of families who are not able to benefit under this scheme as it stands at present. That is also true in Pontiac and several ridings on the Quebec side. If the government is really desirous of finding a solution for the problem of the farmers they should make it possible for all who deserve the name of farmer to benefit.	.
Now I want the Minister of Finance to give me a concrete answer on that very important point. I do not want to be unreasonable, I do not want a settler who has just settled to come within these benefits, but the man I refer to is the farmer who by actual work for the last five or ten years has shown himself to be such. It is possible for the government to be fully protected, there are inspectors on the ground in the different provinces and they can distinguish between the settler and the real farmer. I ask the minister to give a ruling on that point. In my section we are absolutely in favour of anything that will improve the lot of the farmer as well as of the working man, but under this legislation we see no salvation and no help for one of the finest rural sections there is in Canada to-day.

The minister answered me at that time that he was not aware that any representations had been made to the government. After recess the minister was kind enough to refer to a telegram, I believe, sent by the chairman of the board. I did not happen to be in my seat at the time.
Mr. RHODES. Sent by the commissioner. Air. VALLANCE:
In view of fact that Saskatchewan is only province which provides for exemptions from seizure under chattel mortgage and in view of fact that conditions of loan require additional security on chattels, believe board will require legislation in your province which will make security taken on chattels in province of equal value to similar security taken in other provinces.
That suggests to me that the other eight provinces have no such exemption legislation. Saskatchewan did have an exemption law unless legislation passed recently cancelled it. The very fact that we have an exemption law indicates that the farmers in that province probably were in greater need of financial assistance than those in any other province. In spite of what the hon. member for North Huron has said about the western provinces I still claim that we in the west, through no fault of our own, find ourselves in a more difficult position than farmers in the eastern provinces. If this Canadian Farm Loan Act is to be operative in Saskatchewan only on condition that the exemption law now in existence be done away with this act will be of very little advantage to the farmers there. All loans that have been advanced up to the present to farmers in Saskatchewan have been advanced with these exemptions in existence.
What are the exemptions? I put them on record in Hansard last Monday; they are: Four oxen, horses, or mules, or any four of them, six cows, six sheep, four pigs and fifty domestic fowls besides the other animals kept for food purposes, together with food for such animals for the period from November 1, to April 31, or such portions of the months which follow the date of seizure.
Now I am in hearty accord with the act and the spirit of the act and what it proposes to do, but if as a preliminary to its becoming operative in Saskatchewan we are to be compelled to forego that right we had

If they had not had them you would have had, not hundreds but tens of thousands of destitute farmers in Saskatchewan alone. So I am apprehensive about what the final result will be if we should be faced with climatic conditions in the next few years similar to those we have had for the past five or six. So I urge the minister that the exemption laws be left in effect; loans have been advanced by private companies with these exemption laws in existence, and if private capital is willing to invest in farm mortgages notwithstanding the exemption law, surely the Dominion of Canada can do the same. I think section 9 deals with this whole matter. It reads:
In the event of legislation being passed by the legislature of any province operating under this act after loans have been made available in that province which, in the opinion of the board, would prejudicially affect the security of existing or future loans, the board, by notice to be published in the Canada Gazette, may cease to make further loans in that province.
It would seem that this farm loan board is going to be clothed with authority to sit in judgment on the legislatures of the provinces, and if legislation passed by a province does not meet with the approval of the farm loan board that board will have the right to cease lending money in that province. That power to supersede the legislature is too great to give to any board. I urge that before this bill is passed the minister give consideration to those provinces that have exemption laws.

The Country Guide should be good enough authority for the statement I am making, and it says that 85 per cent of the prairie farmers own their farms and only 45 per cent are mortgaged. If I were the Minister of Finance I would not make a loan at all to some of these people in the 45 per cent class. No doubt they are some of those that my hon. friend was referring to who want a loan all the time. You cannot satisfy them with loans, Mr. Chairman. I had only one mortgage left, Mr. Chairman; I had cleaned up all the rest, and I went to the last man who owed me $3,200, the balance on a farm, and I said to him, "I want you to pay me. You have owed me this money for seven years. What are you going to do about it?" "Well," he said, "I can't pay." I said, "I think you can. I hear you made good profits last year, that you had a pretty good crop on this farm. Now I think you had better pay." "Well," he said, "take $1,000 and I will pay it." Now if the Minister of Finance is going to make loans to that type of man that only wants to settle with you for so much, then God help the people who are standing behind this country and buying its securities for their old age. I would be most particular in making a loan to farmers. First I would want to know the man. He would be 50 per cent to start with.
I would look him over, and his ability to farm. Then I would want to look at the farm. You may have good fertile land, but if you have a shiftless, useless individual on that land, your loan is no good.
I have said that 85 per cent of the prairie farmers own their farms. In Ontario 88 per cent of the farmers ow-n their farms, and only 42 per cent of them are mortgaged. So we out west are in just about as good a position as the farmers in the county of my hon. friend from North Huron (Mr. Spotton). I just wanted to make that reference to show that the Ontario farmer is not in a very much better position than we are in western Canada.
The government is paying thousands of dollars to keep up unemployment camps. There is a camp in my constituency with from 1,200 to 1,500 men in it, and they are having the best time of.their lives. They have their hockey matches and their boxing bouts and concerts two or three days a week, and the menu card is as good as you could get at the Chateau Laurier cafeteria. Why keep these young men there? In the pioneer days-yes,

in my day-we got no such pap handed out to us. We went out to fight the battles on the open prairie, and I am glad of the experiences I went through as a pioneer.
This is not my last contribution on the floor of this house; I am going to notify the house of that now. I have heard members around me stating that this is their last contribution in this house, and others expect it to be theirs. Well, this is not my last. Marquette tells me that I have a mission in this house, and that I have got to serve them. I have had letters sent to me and they have encouraged me greatly. There is a new era coming for we have a government that is doing something. For goodness sake, gentlemen opposite, wake up and help solve this country's problems to bring Canada back on its feet. Stop your calamity howling over there, and spread a little sunshine. I look into the faces of hon. gentlemen opposite who are members of the United Farmers. I am a member of the United Farmers of Manitoba, and just as good a one as any that sits on the other side of the house. I have financed and helped them all down through. I believe in them and stand back of them to-day. They have sent a resolution here asking for the abolition of these unemployment camps. They are going back to horses; they are going to farm as the Almighty intended them to farm, but the difficulty is that they cannot hire the labour. The labour is not available. The men are all in the camps enjoying themselves. Let us get back to the right conditions. We have a country that is the best in the world, and I defy anyone, and this includes my hon. friend from Willow Bunch, to challenge that statement. I know the district he comes from; I was in it in the early days. I have a great many friends. in Willow Bunch. I have travelled all over the United States and have seen the conditions there. I know the conditions under which the farmers borrow from the government of the United States under their Fraser-Lemcke act. I have seen the actual conditions of the farmers themselves, and I make this statement, Mr. Chairman, that there is no country in the world that offers the same inducements as Canada to the young man who wants to go out and work. So I say to you young professional men who are struggling for an existence in some country town: Go and get one of those western farms; this is the best time you ever had to buy one of them; take off your coat and go to work and farm it the way the Almighty intended you to farm it.

The hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard has said that it is not necessary to go into the loaning business, that it should be left with private interests. I want to take issue with that statement. It is necessary. Until the Ontario development board started we never had in Ontario sufficient long term, low interest credit to farmers, and that is why they entered the field. That is why this bill has been introduced. It has been introduced to supply that need, and I congratulate the Minister of Finance on its introduction. Perhaps, as the hon. member for West Middlesex has said, a few applications have been granted under the Ontario development board in the last few months. But no applications would have been granted under the Ontario development board had it not been for the action of the Minister of Finance in introducing this bill. The Ontario development board has been negligent in that it has not supplied the need of credit, and it has been negligent also in its failure to send a representative to meet the creditors, under
the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, so that an adjustment could be made. I find that in no instance have any official receivers under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act had representations from the Ontario development board. We have heard hon. members get up and claim that mortgages should be reduced, that there should be a debt reduction, that doctors and lawyers should reduce their fees and storekeepers and mortgage companies should reduce their accounts; yet they are supporting a government that does not recognize the necessity of sending a representative under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act to make a suitable adjustment so that the farmers may be able to pay their debts. In my opinion this act should be worked in conjunction with the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, because I believe that is necessary. I believe there are many private persons who have mortgages on farms and are in need of money, and who would make a settlement of sixty or seventy per cent of their claim if they could get the money, because they are in need of funds at the present time, and this act could be worked in conjunction with that legislation. No loans had been made by the Ontario development board until after the meeting which was referred to by the hon. member for North Huron, the meeting of the United Farmers in convention in Toronto, when they criticized the action of the Ontario government and the fact that they were not making any more loans. If that is so, and if that
condition is general throughout Manitoba, I am glad to hear it; but I am rather of the opinion that Manitoba is not in a much better position than any of the three prairie provinces, or even British Columbia. The figure given by the hon. member showing that eighty-five per cent of the farmers owned their farms is entirely fallacious; and the figure showing that only forty-two per cent of the farms have mortgages is, I claim, also wrong. M e were told by the Prime Minister in his radio addresses-and surely he was pretty careful about what he told the public over the radio-that the farm debt of this country was no less than 81,000,000,000. If the farm debt is as large as that, surely Manitoba has not been the one province that is exempt, May I for a moment refer to a statement made by the hon. member for Yancouver-Burrard who said that the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act was against the best interests of 90 per cent of the farmers of this country. As one who comes from the prairie provinces I have to take exception to that statement. I believe the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act is a very good piece of legislation and one very badly needed in Canada. From recent information I understand that not only is it being used to a considerable extent in the prairie provinces, but in the old province of Quebec it is probably being used more than in any other and I am quite sure it will be used in Manitoba. I also take exception to the statement made by the hon. member that this is class legislation that we have before us. In my opinion the legislation was put forward entirely as a matter of self 
preservation, on the part of the dominion. The 'farmers who represent the greatest calling in this country are a certain asset that we cannot afford to let go into bankruptcy wholesale and we cannot have them leave their farms. It is because of that situation and the fear that that might take place, such legislation as this has been proposed by the government, namely the extension of the farm loan act and the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act.	.	_
The hon. member said also that this financing is being carried out to encourage the farmers in greater production. I do not believe that. I think the Minister of Finance told the house only the other day that this was being done to help out the debt situation throughout the dominion and I believe that statement is correct. We have to-day, as some hon. members have pointed out, an extremely serious debt situation in Canada, particularly with regard to agriculture and it is to help to reduce the terrible debt that the farmers are trying to carry that this act is being passed, so that they may be able to refund their debts through the application of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act and the use of the Canadian Farm Loan Act, thus not only bringing about a smaller liability but having it carried at a much lower rate of interest.
We must remember that during war time the farmers were encouraged to increase their holdings tremendously in support of the interests of Canada as a whole. After the war when we had a seven months' winter so far as the west was concerned, we had a famine in feed which caused enormous debts to be developed amongst the farm communities. We found the price of cattle dropping so rapidly the following year that huge debts were incurred wherever cattle were being carried. The farmers have never got over those times and the legislation before us today would help them considerably toward at least seeing daylight.
So far as agriculture is concerned the problem in Canada both east and west is on the one hand one of prices which have been extremely low, and the fact that agriculture has not been in a position to regulate in any way its prices as has been done with regard to prices for the products of industry. Second, the problem before Canada east and west is one oif debt.
Before I sit down may I refer to a statement made by the hon. member for North Huron whose words I think I caught correctly. He used these words, that when western members spoke about western Canada

Farm Loan Act
they slandered and libelled their own province in referring to the debts of their municipalities and provinces. I think this statement was entirely uncalled -for. I am in pretty steady attendance in this house and so far I have not heard a statement with regard to th-e debts of western Canada made by any western member on either side that was not correct. I think it ill becomes the hon. member to make such a charge. He went on to say that he was glad that by this legislation there was going to be $90,000,000 put at the service of the farm loan 'board and he intimated that this was for Ontario. Even if only part of it was for Ontario, it appears that conditions in that province are not so rosy after all if the farmers there require the assistance that is being proposed by this legislation. The situation in Ontario is the same as it is in western Canada so far as agriculture is concerned; it is one of low prices over which the farmer has no control and this has brought about the huge amount of debt that agriculture is carrying.

speechtext: Of course, Mr. Chairman, we will have this discussion all over again when we come to the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, but we have covered quite a wide field so I have no objection to answering the question of my hon. friend. The official receiver has no authority to do anything except to attempt to bring the parties together in a mutual arrangement. But the board of review, the case having been referred to it, has authority to order a compromise which would involve a reduction in the amount of the mortgage held by the provincial board.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: This act has just been introduced in the province of Prince Edward Island, and naturally we are receiving many questions and a great deal of correspondence in regard to it. The difficulty seems to be that the man who needs assistance most will not be able to get it under this act. I refer to the man who is mortgaged pretty heavily, perhaps beyond the point at which the farm loan board would give him assistance if they adhere to the limit of sixty-six per cent of the value of the property. The man who has a gilt edged risk does not have so much difficulty in obtaining a loan as the man who is loaded up a little beyond that point, but the second man is the one who needs assistance at the present time. We are led to understand, by the minister's statement, that the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act and this act are distinctly separate, and that they cannot be termed even companionable acts.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Then perhaps they may
be termed companionable acts, but even if a man has an arrangement made under the other act so far as I can see there is no way by which he can get new money under this act with which to carry on. On previous occasions the minister has explained that it is not wise to put in the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act any provision which would compel the farm loan board to lend money to anyone who might be suggested or recommended under the other measure. I quite agree that there is room for argument there, but still there is a great difficulty. If a man
makes 'an arrangement with his creditors under the other act he is unable to get any new money from the man who holds the mortgage, or from any other man or from any lawyer who has money to loan, and in Prince Edward Island we do not have loan companies. So it is impossible for a farmer to get a loan under any condition. That is the difficulty; even if the farmer makes an arrangement with his creditors he cannot get money with which to carry on. If something could be worked out under which the man who is hard up and cannot meet his interest or principal payments could 'be tided over and given a new start it would be 'a good thing, and, I think, in keeping with the intention of these two pieces of legislation.
I am glad the minister gave us the explanation he did give this afternoon; we will be able to send copies of Hansard to those who are interested. I do hope that in handling these loans through the representatives in the different provinces the government will be as lenient as possible. Do I understand from the minister that this sixty-six per cent is on the real estate alone, or does it include movables and personal property?

That is on the real estate, and that has reference to the first and second mortgage. But I pointed out to my hon. friend from Hants-Kings a few moments ago that whereas hitherto a first mortgage has been limited to fifty per cent of the value of the land and twenty per cent of the value of the buildings, under an amendment which I propose to move when I have an opportunity to do so that percentage will be increased enab" ling us to loan up to fifty per cent of the value of the land and buildings. So in that respect I may point out to my hon. friend, who may not have been here the other day, that we are going even further than they have gone in the United States, where at the moment they are confining themselves to our old limit of fifty per	cent of	the value	of	theland and twenty per	cent of	the value	of	the
buildings.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
There is one matter I
should like to draw	to the	attention	of	theminister, arising out	of the	definition	of	the
word "farmer." This afternoon the minister was kind enough to restate what he told the house on Monday, namely that it was his intention to bring in an amendment to the present definition of the word "farmer" which will provide that under the farm loan act the definition will be the same as under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. Members of the committee will, I think, recall that
Farm Loan Act

the object of having that definition standardized was that there are certain farmers who live in small towns or village, some of whom have retired, who still have to live on the earnings of their farms, and it seems that they were not in a position to obtain loans under the act. This morning I received a wire which I think will prove of interest to the minister, which reads as follows:
Board of review holds opinion that present definition of farmer would not cover ease where party does not actually till the soil.
This is from Alberta. If it is so that the board of review in that province holds that the definition under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act requires that a man should actually till the soil, then that definition is not going to be very acceptable since it does not cover the cases which the committee intended should be covered when it was suggested that the definition should be changed. I quite recognize that it does not necessarily follow that the farm loan board in its operations will interpret the word "farmer" as it has been interpreted under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, but I think we should keep in mind that it is highly desirable that the definition should be interpreted in practically the same way. I can quite conceive that later on, if this definition is interpreted by the farm loan board as it has been by the board of review in Alberta, applicants who reside in a village and are not actually tilling the soil will not be eligible for loans under this act.
I commend to the minister's consideration this interpretation by the board of review of Alberta before he actually brings in his amendment with respect to the definition of the word "farmer" because I think it essential that this definition should be so couched as definitely to provide that a farmer, so long as he is a farmer, does not actually have to reside on the land proposed as security; nor should it be necessary for him personally to be tilling it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Of course the logical thing would be to discuss the definition of farmer when we come to that section, but as I say we 'have travelled so far afield over a number of days that we might as well keep at it until we have answered every possible query that may arise, so I do not take exception to my hon. friend having raised the point. The definition of " farmer " as given in the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act is I think as broad and comprehensive a definition as it would be possible to provide. I give that view to the committee in all humility and with due deference to hon. members learned

in the law who have had a wider experience than I have had. My experience has been that the simpler a definition is made the more comprehensive it becomes, and that the more one attempts to include exceptional cases the more it is restricted. There will always be border-line cases. By using the definition of " farmer " as it appears in the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act there will be no restriction calling for actual occupation of the soil on the part of the individual, so long as he is a bona fide farmer. I believe the hon. member raised the question whether or not a person could be said to be tilling the soil. My answer would be that if he is not tilling the soil he is not a farmer. I would add however that in defining a term borderline cases will always be found, and I believe we will have to leave to the discretion of the farm loan board the matter of dealing with individual cases. They will have to decide, on the merits of each case, whether or not a man is a bona fide farmer and entitled to a loan on his farm.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: What about the man who is a poultry farmer or a bee keeper? Certainly he would not be tilling the soil, but he is none the less a farmer engaged in a certain class of farming.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

May I answer the hon. member as I did another hon. member? I do not believe I am called upon to state whether or not a certain individual shall come within the definition of the word " farmer." Parliament will say what in its judgment is a farmer, and following that the board in its discretion must determine whether or not an individual case comes within the law as laid down by parliament. I believe upon reflection the hon. member will realize that the condition I have described must obtain. If I wanted to find the definition of the term " farmer " after parliament had expressed itself I would refer to the Department of Justice. I would most respectfully decline however to place myself in the position of interpreting the law applicable to individual cases.

My amendment, Mr. Chairman, which I will ask the chairman to read, has a twofold purpose. Under the act as it exists an initial advance of 85,000,000 was made to the board by the government, upon which the board under the statute as it exists is obliged to pay interest to the government at the rate of five per cent. This amendment is designed to make it within the power of the governor in council to fix the rate of interest, the object being to reduce that rate of interest to the general level of the rate of interest which will be charged on all loans.
There is a further amendment by adding a subsection 4 to section 3, reading as follows:
The hoard may retire the outstanding capital stock subscribed by borrowers under the act, by crediting the amount of the par value of the stock subscribed by the borrower as a payment upon the borrower's indebtedness under his loan from the board, and when so credited, the borrower shall thereupon cease to be a stockholder of the board.
As I understand it, in layman's language that simply means this, that whereas hitherto the farmer who has received a loan from the board had to subscribe to the stock to the value of five per cent and had to pay interest upon that sum until such time as the mortgage was finally liquidated, this amendment will have the effect of immediately crediting that five per cent to his loan from the board and he will have the benefit of the interest on that between now and the time when the mortgage is finally paid.

17. Subsections one and two of section nine of The Canadian Farm Loan Act Amendment Act, 1934, renumbered as section nineteen of the Canadian Farm Loan Act, are repealed and the following are substituted therefor:
"(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in Part I of this act, the board may in any case where it lends on the security of a first mortgage, make a further loan for a period of not more than six years, repayable on such terms as the board may determine, on the security of a second mortgage on the farm lands and in those provinces of Canada where chattel security may be taken by the board, of a charge on live stock and other personal property.
(2) The aggregate of loans made to any one borrower under the provisions of parts I and
II	of this act shall not exceed, in those provinces of Canada where chattel security may be taken by the board, two-thirds of the appraised value of the land and buildings in respect of which security is taken and in any province where chattel security may not be taken sixty per cent of the said value and shall not exceed at any one time the sum of seven thousand five hundred dollars. The amount advanced' under this section shall not exceed one-half of the amount advanced on the security of the first mortgage."
The principal effect of this amendment is to provide that in Quebec where we may not take a chattel mortgage, the position shall not be prejudiced on that account, and therefore we make an arbitrary figure of sixty per cent as against sixty-six and two-thirds per cent where we can take chattel mortgages.

speechtext: I am advised that practically the only instances in which the farm loan1 board' have asked a farmer for security by way of chattel mortgage, where they held a mortgage on his farm which was in arrears, were not with the object of further involving the farmer in debt to the board but to protect him against attempts on the part of other creditors to cripple him by securing a mortgage on his chattels. subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext: I am very much in accord with the amendment the minister has proposed, as to lending up to two-thirds of the value; I think that is sufficient. But in my province and in the particular part I represent there are many farmers operating a section or a section and a half or two sections. Assume that the appraised value is $20 an acre; two-thirds of that would figure out at $8,500 on a section. So that if the aggregate is limited to $7,500, there will be many farmers whose needs that would not meet. Within the last ten or fifteen years loans have been made in that part of the country based on valuations of S30 to $40 an acre, and in many cases loans of fifty per cent of that value have been made. I think two-thirds of the appraised value is sufficiently high, but many farmers will be unable to take advantage of the act because $7,500 would not be enough on the larger farms. Many farmers have loans of $10,000 on a section of land, and the moral risk in many of those cases is just as good as it would be for $7,500 on a smaller area. Many farmers out there who are farming a section or more are better farmers than those working on three-quarters of a section. Does the minister not think that that limit might be increased if the security is there?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FACILITATE AND INCREASE THE EXTENSION OF CREDIT TO FARMERS
speechtext:
It is a question of policy. The idea we had was that a greater service would be done by helping a larger number of small farmers rather than by using up the amount available in a smaller number of large mortgages. While no doubt there will be cases where worthy farmers will suffer by not

being able to secure a larger loan, on balance I have no doubt that a greater public service will be rendered by spreading the money over a larger number of small loans. After all, while there are conditions peculiar to the prairies, we must remember that this legislation is applicable to all Canada, and in the great majority of provinces when you get beyond $7,500 you are dealing not with a farmer but with an enterprise. So on balance it was felt that we could not go beyond a maximum of $7,500.

I have in mind a man who has a section of land lying very close to town, land which in ordinary times would be valuable. I believe there is about $14,000 standing against it, and the man who holds the claim against it has said to the owner, " If you can get me the cash I will take fifty per cent of what you owe me, because I need the money." The man who owns the property is about seventy years of age, is living in town, and has a tenant on the farm. I should like to see the definition of the word "farmer" left in such a way that it would be within the option of the board to make a loan. In the case to which I have made reference the man is too old to take over the operation of the farm, and it is much better for him to have it in the hands of a tenant. The tenant could not possibly buy it and obtain a loan. I believe it would be wise to leave the definition as wide open as possible, so that these matters may be left to the decision of the board. If we have the right kind of board I believe justice would be done, and they would be in a better position to deal with the needs of each farming community.

This is an item I wish to refer to because it represents a set of items of which this one is typical. It is a vote for improvements and repairs to dominion public buildings, and the vote is increased from $40,000 last year to $50,000 this .year. In view of the money that is being expended under the Public Works Construction Act I submit we should not be increasing year by year the amount that can be spent under a special vote of this kind. It places upon the officials of the department and the minister the obligation to meet demands that would not be
made upon them if there were not these amounts placed in the estimates which they can allocate anywhere. In speaking of that I refer generally to items of this kind. Public works estimates should be kept down as far as possible to what are actually known as public works estimates which are passed on by this committee of the House of Commons, instead of their being passed on by the officials of the department without the members of this committee knowing the places to which those amounts are going.

The objection,
if I may so term it, raised by my hon. friend is met I think by the practice of the department in years gone by. The procedure is that the chief architect obtains from the district architects from time to time estimates of the amounts likely to be required for repairs to the buildings in the different districts; he assembles those amounts and in the light of experience over a period of years determines what is a fair and reasonable amount to ask for this work. My hon. friend will agree that it is impossible to foresee everything that may happen. A roof may be found to be leaking, a heating system may fail, or any other part of a building may require attention. As my hon. friend knows, during the last three or four years the necessity for economy has curtailed the amounts of these votes. In 1930-31, for instance, the appropriation was 855.500 for the corresponding item, and our experience has been that in the past few years we have not had quite as much at our command as the circumstances required. For that reason this vote has been slightly increased.

We shall perhaps be able to facilitate the work of the committee if we get as much information as we can beforehand in connection with the works that are being carried on under the Public Works Construction Act. I understand that under that act a large amount of money is given in a lump sum just as this is, without being allotted to any particular work, and that out of that lump sum large scale improvements have been made this year in order to get the buildings in as good a shape as possible. A much larger amount has been at the discretion of the minister under that act during the last year than ever before, and for that reason there is much less necessity for any increase in these lump sums in the estimates this year.
There are certain things that I think this committee should perhaps reserve until we discuss the Public Works Construction Act. I

at the moment to take up the time of the committee with any further protest except in regard to each of these lump sum items. I think the increases in them are all wrong. The principle is wrong. I am told, and it is quite apparent from some of the orders in council that have been passed under the Public Works Construction Act, that buildings are being erected and sites purchased for buildings without this house passing upon the advisability of placing those buildings there or of purchasing those sites. I do not think it can be defended, and it is contrary to all the principles of public works construction. Take any building, I do not care in what province it may be; this house has a right to pass upon it. It should not be passed upon by the officials of this department nor by the minister nor by council without that item having been passed upon in committee of the whole house, as has been the practice since confederation until within the last year or two.

I assume that this amount is here for the general maintenance and upkeep of public buildings. In the last four or five years it has been annually decreasing until there was no money to maintain these buildings. May I thank the Ministel of Public Works for the item of $139,000 for the enlargement of the wharf at Riviere du Loup. I deeply appreciate the consideration the minister has given to that beautiful place on the south shore of the river St. Lawrence known as Riviere du Loup. The amount voted for the enlargement of the wharf is substantial. What amount will be spent for steel, what amount for lumber, and what amount for labour?

This is an important wharf over which there is a heavy volume of traffic. I cannot state definitely how much steel or timber will be required; that is a matter to be determined after the plans have been prepared. The figure appearing in the vote is a rough estimate of the amount which will be required to do the work.

I understand betweer
$85,000 and $90,000 will be spent for steel.
My information shows that sheet steel piling will cost about $79,000.

That is satisfactory, and
I thank the hon. gentleman. I highly appreciate the way the minister has dealt with the member for Temiscouata since he has been minister. May I tell him that I know he put that amount in the estimates in appreciation of the savings that I helped him to make in his own department when I told him what was going on in the sale of materials, and which resulted in substantial sums of money being refunded to the department. I told him also of what was going on in other constituencies where some people were selling rotten timber for wharves, and he was kind enough to send the chief engineer there and to have all the rock fill taken out from the wharf in order that the lumber might be tested to the bottom. That meant a great saving to the department, and it is because of that the minister has put this amount in the estimates. There is something else. The government has lent a big amount of money to Newfoundland. That was denounced here and the government did not lend any more after I denounced it; they were so thankful to me for telling them the right thing to do that they said, "Well, Temiscouata, you have saved us millions of dollars through our not lending any more money to Newfoundland, and we will give you something for your wharf at Riviere du Loup." I thank the minister and the government for what they have done in appreciation of the work the Liberals are doing.

I am not sure

Can the minister give
me any information regarding the enlargement of the wharf at Pointe au Pic, the contract for which was let last fall? I am told that the firm of Hill & Sibbald, of St. Catharines, Ontario, got the contract, but did not go on with the construction of the work, and that afterwards some other firm was to have been given the contract because the first contractors would not undertake the work for certain reasons; I do not know what they were. I should like to know who really has the contract for the construction of that wharf, and if the work is to go on, and if so when it is to be done?

The firm to
whom the contract was awarded is the one mentioned by my hon. friend, Hill & Sibbald. The department has nothing to indicate that they will not go on with the work. Recent correspondence indicates that they have ordered their sheet piling, and so far as we know they propose going on with the work.
When will it be proceeded with-next spring?
At the opening of navigation.

When my hon. friend
speaks of sheet piling, may I ask if this is not the first time that sheet piling has been used for that purpose in that district? I do not think it has ever been used for work such as that down below Quebec.

I do not know
of any instance in which sheet piling has been used in that locality, but it is not an experiment at all.

What I want to know
from the minister is whether sheet piling has been tested in construction of this nature below Quebec. I have never heard' of its being used in that district, although it may have been used elsewhere. Are there any other wharves below Quebec in which sheet piling has been used?

I can only say
that in the opinion of the engineers of the department it is a sound and safe and suitable type of work for that locality.

I should like to take
advantage of this opportunity to bring to the attention of the minister the situation at Bayfield. I have had some correspondence with him and I am glad to note that there is indication of some intention to do some dredging there and also to make further repairs to the pier. I have talked with the fishermen and they are firmly of the opinion that until the breakwater that was destroyed some years ago is restored, conditions will not be good. When I was in London last year the engineer gave me an estimate of 812,000 as the cost of restoring the ninety feet of breakwater that was washed away some years ago. If that work were done it would be money well spent and would result in a saving of money in the future.
